title: Adaptability-focused debrief: Juno Lam (runtime eng exercise)
content:
Quick take:
Juno shows strong practical instincts for debugging production inference issues and a clear preference for shipping small iterative fixes rather than over-architecting. Very comfortable reading perf traces and hypothesizing root causes quickly. They are less fluent in some of our orchestration primitives (policy-driven routing, autoscaler knobs) but expressed an eagerness to learn and had concrete ideas to get up to speed.

Evidence / notable bits from loop:
- Live debug exercise (p99 spikes): identified KV cache miss hotspots and a batching corner case within ~20 minutes. Suggested adding a low-overhead per-model prefix cache + metric, which is pragmatic.
- Code exercise: wrote readable C++-wrapper/pybind sketch for a tiny tokenizer integration; had syntactic rough edges but solid design.
- Systems Q: when asked about rollbacks and fallback model variants, proposed a multi-tier fallback with circuit-breaker on latency percentiles, but missed cost-accounting nuance (quantization variant tradeoffs).
- Communication: concise, asked clarifying questions early, and iterated on toy repro to validate hypothesis.

Strengths:
- Fast blameless debugging: pattern recognition for perf traces and NVTX-like markers.
- Pragmatic tradeoffs: often proposes incremental instrumentation + short-term mitigation before big refactors.
- Learning momentum: gave a 3-point plan for learning our infra (read book-keeping guides, instrument two live routes, pair with SRE for 2 weeks).

Weaknesses / risks:
- Limited exposure to fleet autoscaling policies used in Dedicated (has k8s autoscaler experience but not traffic-class autoscalers).
- Some gaps in cost modeling — initially optimized purely for latency without demonstrating strong unit-cost reasoning.
- Implementation polish: prototypes look correct but need more attention to concurrency edge cases.

Suggested homework (realistic & low friction):
- "profile-and-patch": given a small LLM model serving repo, add lightweight prefix cache metrics, reproduce a KV-miss spike, and submit a short PR with a mitigation + benchmark. Target: 3-5 hours.
- Bonus: write 4 bullets on how batching window sizes should adapt to tail-latency objectives vs token-cost budgets.

Interview scores (heuristic, my scale 1-5):
- Adaptability / learning speed: 5/5
- Debugging & perf intuition: 5/5
- System design at runtime scale: 4/5
- Implementation quality: 3/5
- Communicates tradeoffs: 4/5

Recommendation and level tilt:
- Lean hire. Recommend IC3 (senior engineer) with a 3-month ramp plan focusing on autoscaler primitives and cost-accounting. Strong match for short-term needs on perf triage and runtime incident mitigation.

Onboarding suggestions if hired:
- Week 1: pair shadow on two incident postmortems, read our compile/kernel selection notes, setup dev cluster.
- Week 2-4: ownership of one low-traffic route, implement a KV-prefetch/instrumentation ticket.
- Month 1-3: pair on Dedicated autoscaler policy; rotate through on-call for two weeks with SRE mentor.

Open questions to resolve in debrief:
- How comfortable are we letting an IC3 own production routing policy changes in month 2? (Ops-level risk)
- If homework shows polish issues, is there appetite for a slightly more junior comp band?

Notes to self: check with Maya on whether we need explicit quantization-cost rubric before extending offer. Also sync with Aurora on adding a small benchmark to the homework repo so candidates can self-validate.

Next steps: send homework + 48-hour turnaround request; schedule follow-up with hiring panel to decide ticketing and level.

-- Liam
